summary: Lays out a framework for PSAMP, a protocol for picking out some packets from a stream, forming reports about them, and exporting those reports to a collector. It describes the components involved, such as the selection steps, and how they fit together.

plainLanguage.summary: Packet Sampling (PSAMP) selects some packets from a network stream and sends reports about them to a collector. This RFC describes the system's parts and the information reports should contain.

questions: how does packet sampling and reporting work
subtitle: A framework for selecting packets, creating reports, and exporting them for network measurement.

tldr.problem: Network operators need consistent traffic measurements, but examining every packet can be costly and vendor-specific.
tldr.mechanism: PSAMP separates packet selection, metering and report creation, then export to a collector, with generic requirements for each stage.
tldr.outcome: The framework defines terms and requirements; companion RFCs describe selection techniques, export protocol, and information model.

today: RFC 5474 is Informational and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The companion documents for selection, export, and the information model are RFC 5475, RFC 5476, and RFC 5477.

sections.title: Purpose of the PSAMP Framework
sections.content:
The Packet SAMPling (PSAMP) framework describes how network elements select packets and export reports about them to a collector. The goal is consistent measurement across equipment from different vendors.

Selection includes random sampling, deterministic filtering, and deterministic approximations to random sampling such as hash-based selection. The detailed selection techniques, export protocol, and information model are described in companion RFCs 5475, 5476, and 5477.
sections.plainLanguage: PSAMP helps network equipment choose packets to measure and report them in a consistent way. The framework covers more than random sampling.

sections.title: Observation, Selection, Metering, and Export
sections.content:
An Observation Point is where packets enter the measurement system. A Selection Process decides which packets to select. The Metering Process uses each selected packet to construct a report, and the Exporting Process sends reports to a Collector.

A report stream contains packet reports and report interpretation, which describes how to interpret them. A Selection Process may chain selectors, with the output from one selector becoming the input to the next.
sections.plainLanguage: The system observes packets, selects some, creates reports, and sends those reports to a collector. The report stream also explains how to interpret the results.

sections.title: Requirements for Selection and Reporting
sections.content:
Selectors should be simple enough to run at line rate, support different measurement needs, and work with IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS. Selection should resist packet streams crafted to evade measurement or overload the system. A device may run multiple independent Metering Processes.

Reports should be self-defining, allow information loss to be detected, and include enough information to assess measurement accuracy. Reported treatment information should reflect the router state seen by the packet. Full capture of arbitrary packet streams is outside the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Packet selection should be fast and robust. Reports should explain themselves and reveal when data may have been lost.

sections.title: Selectors, Reports, and Export
sections.content:
Selectors may filter packets by their content or use sampling methods such as count-based, time-based, probabilistic, or hash-based selection. Primitive selectors count their input packets and report sequence numbers, which help estimate the selection fraction even when reports are lost.

Packet reports include selector sequence numbers and the identity of the Metering Process. Optional fields may describe packet headers, treatment, timestamps, or hashes. PSAMP uses IPFIX for export; export must avoid congestion, allow buffering delay to be limited, and provide security options.
sections.plainLanguage: A selector can choose packets by rules or by a sampling method. Sequence numbers help a collector notice missing reports and understand the measurement.

sections.title: Applications and Security
sections.content:
The RFC describes applications including baseline measurement, drill-down into selected traffic, trajectory sampling across observation points, passive performance measurement, and troubleshooting. These uses depend on accurate reports and clear interpretation data.

Packet reports can expose packet content, so their confidentiality matters. Hash-based selection can be manipulated if attackers learn its parameters; the RFC recommends keeping those parameters private and changing them regularly. Export security relies on IPFIX mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements can help operators understand traffic and find faults. They must also protect report contents and keep selection secrets from attackers.
